source.title: Cyclic Sparse Training: Is it Enough?
source.authors: A. Gadhikar; Sree Harsha Nelaturu; Rebekka Burkholz

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper; no material truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own experiments on how cyclic training and pruning affect generalization, and argues that cyclic optimization rather than sparsity-induced regularization explains much of iterative pruning's performance. These results refine the generalization claim but do not test any listed version directly.
record.gate_note: The paper tests cyclic training and sparse-mask/pruning combinations on image classification. It does not report experiments on random-label memorization, width sweeps, convolutional versus fully connected models, optimizer comparisons, batch-size changes, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness measures, or removing memorized examples. Figure-only performance curves are not reconstructed as numeric rows; values used to choose training cycles are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study measures cyclic learning-rate schedules, sparse masks and pruning performance, rather than any listed claim version. Its Hessian eigenvalue analysis does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or rank generalization gaps, so it does not test V7. Batch size and optimizer are fixed; partial label corruption does not test V1's random-label memorization comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors argue that cyclic training explains a substantial share of iterative pruning's performance through improved optimization. At high sparsity, they identify coupling between initialization and mask as a remaining requirement. They propose SCULPT-ing to improve this coupling and reduce computational costs; it matches LRR in some settings, while standalone SCULPT-ing remains below LRR on CIFAR-10. Escape from local optima and flatter neighborhoods are proposed mechanisms, not established causal explanations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates cyclic training, pruning at initialization, iterative pruning, and a proposed sparse cyclic pruning procedure. These are distinct from the claim versions' specified interventions and comparisons.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with sparsity and number of training cycles; the text also states that the relative performance of cyclic training and LRR differs between low and high sparsity.

fits_no_version.finding: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet20, cyclic random-mask training exceeds LRR at 59% sparsity (92.20% versus 92.00% at matched cycles), but falls below it at 79% and 95% sparsity, including at reported peak performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cyclic sparse training's performance relative to iterative pruning depends on sparsity and training-cycle budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3 reports decreasing maximum Hessian eigenvalues during cyclic training and interprets this as a flatter neighborhood accompanying improved generalization. These eigenvalues are not magnitude-aware sharpness measurements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cyclic training can accompany lower Hessian-based curvature and improved held-out performance in dense and sparse ResNet20 networks on CIFAR-10.

record.problems: The numeric comparison in Table 1 is limited to CIFAR10 and a ResNet20. The paper states that results generally use means and 95% confidence intervals over 3 seeds, with exceptions, but Table 1 does not provide uncertainty for its entries. Other central comparisons are presented in figures and their exact values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-based accuracy, loss, Hessian, and mask-comparison results are described qualitatively or shown only in figures; exact values are not stated in text and were not reconstructed. The cycle counts in Table 1 are included as conditions, not as separate outcomes. Sign-recovery overlap results in Appendix A.1 were omitted because they measure sign overlap rather than held-out error or the train-test gap.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout, including interactions with training-set size, augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps among similarly fitted networks, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: T5 is inappropriate because the challenged hypothesis concerns pruning-induced regularization, not a listed version. All nine numeric values match Table 1, but their observed/partial states describe an unrelated method comparison. No additional result bearing on V1–V8 requires a missing-row entry.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under different tuning regimes.
Large-batch versus small-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout and weight-decay effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a measure that tracks the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test accuracy.
